newsitem.title: UK: GNI expects cocoa to rally on likely supply gap.
newsitem.headline: GNI expects cocoa to rally on likely supply gap.

text.p: Brokers GNI on Tuesday projected a climb in LIFFE second-month cocoa prices to at least 1,050 stg and up to 1,600 stg over coming months due to a possibly sizeable supply deficit.
Its forecast, which many traders dismissed, also reflected a buying spree scenario that could arise if one trade house with large physical stocks continues to holds on to its position.
"Clearly the market is ripe for a major price move," said GNI in an annual commodity review.

Its lower price estimate, which still implies a rally from the current level of 873 stg of the March contract, was based on the possibility of a surge in West African arrivals in January and February.

"Should they maintain their current low rates...prices could surge to 1,200. Should panic set in, or unexpected tightness evolve because of the inventory held by a trade house...then a surge to 1,600 per tonne could be seen," it said.

World cocoa supply could post a deficit of 180,000 tonnes in 1996/97 (Oct/Sept) compared with an estimated surplus of 161,000 tonnes in 1995/96, reducing world stocks to 34 percent of annual consumption from 42 percent, it said.
But it stressed that the margin of error remained high until the end of January when arrivals should reveal a more accurate picture.

The unusual difficulty of drawing a safe outlook this year stems from the bumper West African harvest of 1995/96 which forecasters still can't decide whether to associate with fluke weather, the sudden maturity of new plantations or structural improvements in purchasing.
GNI put Ivory Coast's total output at around 950,000 tonnes, down from 1.20 million, implying that last year's record crop was more likely to be one-off.

Production trends were similar in Ghana, Ivory Coast and Cameroon but it was very unlikely that an identical degree of investment in the tree population should occur in the same year with similar yields.
Ivory Coast's historical output trend, excluding the 1995/96 crop, signalled a crop of 892,000 tonnes for 1996/97, it said.

But there were other factors at force. Ivorian purchases were concentrated on a few large buyers who pay cash directly to farmers. The process has cut out the middle man and increased the incentive to maximise the crop size.

"The concentration of buyers also means that arrivals figures are probably more accurate. While this could lead to an increase in the estimate of crop size, it could also simply mean that production has been underestimated in previous years," GNI said.
The 1995/96 outturn could have also included large carryover stocks from previous years.
GNI forecast the global crop at 2.559 million tonnes from 2.856 million in 1995/96 including Ghana at 340,000 tonnes, Indonesia 318,000 and Brazil at 199,000 tonnes.
On the consumption side, the growth of world grindings were expected to moderate to 1.65 percent implying a total figure of 2.739 million tonnes, from a massive 7.14 percent surge last season.
But the deficit figure of 180,000 tonnes should be regarded as a mid-point of the likely outcome with the range being between 110,000 and 250,000 tonnes.
